paper_title: Novel or Not? PatEx-Gym: Agentic Prior-Art Search for Novelty Assessment in Patent Examination

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Patent examination is a challenging real-world task that requires agents to discover sparse prior art, iteratively refine queries, inspect technical evidence, and produce novelty assessments documented in Office Actions (OAs) across heterogeneous scientific and technical domains. However, existing benchmarks largely focus on static and limited candidate sets, leaving the full search--reasoning--assessment process underexplored. We present PatEx-Gym, the first framework for developing and evaluating agents for patent examination, which integrates three components. First, PatEx-Bench provides 1K realistic examination tasks, two large-scale retrieval corpora containing over 1M patents and 52K scientific papers, and a harness runtime supporting iterative search, document visits, reasoning, and OA generation. Second, we introduce PASS, an annotation-free Prior-Art Agentic Search Trajectory Synthesis framework. Specifically, it exploits document visits as implicit relevance signals and evidence-acquisition anchors to model intra-turn query behavior, inter-turn search progression, and trajectory-level evidence and outcome quality, yielding PatEx-SynData. Third, we train PatEx-Agent at the 4B scale via supervised fine-tuning on the curated trajectories, establishing a lightweight baseline. Extensive experiments show that final decision accuracy alone does not fully reflect examination quality, while prior-art discovery remains difficult even for strong frontier models. Our PatEx-Agent achieves competitive performance against substantially larger general-purpose agents. These results show that training on PatEx-SynData enables a compact 4B model to serve as a competitive baseline for prior-art search and patent examination. We view patent examination as a demanding testbed for agentic search and deep research agents.

PatEx-Gym: Agentic Prior-Art Search for Novelty Assessment in Patent Examination Qiyao Wang1,2, Xinyi Chen3, Hongbo Wang1,3, Jiayuan Lu3, Jianhang Li3, Minghuan Tan1, Yuan Lin3, Min Yang1,4 1 Shenzhen Institute of Advanced Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences 2 University of Chinese Academy of Sciences Dalian University of Technology 3 # wangqiyao25@mails.ucas.ac.cn # zhlin@dlut.edu.cn # min.yang@siat.ac.cn (cid:209) Website PatRe Shenzhen University of Advanced Technology Corresponding Authors. Equal Contribution. 4 Abstract Patent examination is challenging real-world task that requires agents to discover sparse prior art, iteratively refine queries, inspect technical evidence, and produce novelty assessments documented in Office Actions (OAs) across heterogeneous scientific and technical domains. However, existing benchmarks largely focus on static and limited candidate sets, leaving the full searchreasoningassessment process underexplored. We present PatEx-Gym, the first framework for developing and evaluating agents for patent examination, which integrates three components. First, PatEx-Bench provides 1K realistic examination tasks, two large-scale retrieval corpora containing over 1M patents and 52K scientific papers, and harness runtime supporting iterative search, document visits, reasoning, and OA generation. Second, we introduce PASS, an annotation-free Prior-Art Agentic Search Trajectory Synthesis framework. Specifically, it exploits document visits as implicit relevance signals and evidence-acquisition anchors to model intra-turn query behavior, inter-turn search progression, and trajectory-level evidence and outcome quality, yielding PatEx-SynData. Third, we train PatEx-Agent at the 4B scale via supervised fine-tuning on the curated trajectories, establishing lightweight baseline. Extensive experiments show that final decision accuracy alone does not fully reflect examination quality, while prior-art discovery remains difficult even for strong frontier models. Our PatEx-Agent achieves competitive performance against substantially larger general-purpose agents. These results show that training on PatEx-SynData enables compact 4B model to serve as competitive baseline for prior-art search and patent examination. We view patent examination as demanding testbed for agentic search and deep research agents. 1. Introduction Information retrieval systems have long served as fundamental gateway to information access, spanning general-purpose Web search [Brin and Page, 1998, Burges et al., 2005] and domain-specific search engines in knowledge-intensive fields such as law [Feng et al., 2024, Harvey AI, 2026], education [Usta et al., 2021], finance [Choe et al., 2025], and intellectual property (IP) [Roda et al., 2009]. With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), the paradigm of information access is gradually shifting from discriminative relevance estimation [Robertson et al., 1994, Salton and Buckley, 1988] over in-domain corpora toward generative [Li et al., 2025] and agentic search paradigm [Du et al., 2026b, Ning et al., 2026]. This shift is particularly consequential for patent examination, where reliable novelty assessment fundamentally depends on discovering and reasoning over evidence from large-scale prior-art corpora. Patent examination is inherently knowledge-intensive information access task [Wang et al., 2026b]. To assess the novelty of an application, examiners must discover relevant evidence from massive collections of prior art rather than relying on pre-identified references. They then analyze the retrieved prior art against claim limitations to determine whether the invention has been previously Novel or Not? PatEx-Gym: Agentic Prior-Art Search for Novelty Assessment in Patent Examination Figure 1 Overview of the Harness Runtime in PatEx-Gym, supporting iterative reasoning, prior-art retrieval, document inspection, and OA generation. 𝑟𝑡, 𝑢𝑡, and 𝑧𝑡 denote the reasoning, tool call, and tool results at step 𝑡, respectively. disclosed [Knappich et al., 2026]. This goes beyond fine-grained relevance matching [Ni et al., 2024, Risch et al., 2020] or reasoning [Lim et al., 2025, Wang et al., 2026b] over given prior-art documents: novelty assessment in patent examination requires discovering relevant prior art from large search space and using intermediate findings to guide subsequent search, claim-level comparison, and generate an Office Action (OA)-style report under relevant legal constraints [Setchi et al., 2021]. Such process naturally forms tight searchreasoningassessment loop, making patent examination particularly challenging setting for agentic search. Recent efforts have progressively shifted patent novelty assessment toward more realistic examination settings. HUPD [Suzgun et al., 2023] formulated patent examination as application-level acceptance prediction, while IPBench [Wang et al., 2026a] evaluated the patent examination and classification capabilities of LLMs. PANORAMA [Lim et al., 2025], in contrast, decomposed claim-level examination into prior-art retrieval, relevant-paragraph identification, and novelty or non-obviousness classification. More recent work further emphasizes fine-grained and process-oriented evaluation: FiNE-Patents [Knappich et al., 2026] assesses feature-level passage retrieval and novelty reasoning, while PatRe [Wang et al., 2026b] models the multi-turn lifecycle of OA generation and applicant rebuttal. Existing benchmarks remain static and narrowly scoped relative to realistic examination: they evaluate examination components in isolation, constrain retrieval to small predefined candidate pools, or assume access to relevant prior art. As result, they cannot capture the adaptive and iterative search, evidence discovery, and reasoning required in realistic patent examination. To address these gaps, we present PatEx-Gym, to the best of our knowledge, the first framework for developing and evaluating agents for novelty-oriented prior-art search and reasoning, with generated OAs serving as downstream signal of novelty assessment. Specifically, it integrates three core components that unify benchmarking, scalable trajectory synthesis, and supervised agent training within single framework, as illustrated in Figure 1. Beyond evaluating final OA alone, our PatEx-Gym exposes the complete searchreasoningassessment process, enabling both fine-grained search behavior analysis and the construction of high-quality trajectory for training stronger patent examination agents. More importantly, PatEx-Gym also serves as challenging testbed for general search agents, since its broad coverage across IPC sections naturally spans heterogeneous scientific and technical domains, requiring agents to perform cross-domain query adaptation, tool use, evidence integration, technical reasoning, and report generation. Our main contributions are as follows: We introduce PatEx-Bench, the first benchmark for agentic prior-art search and novelty assessment in patent examination scenario, comprising 1K realistic tasks. Its supported by large-scale Patent1M, Paper-52K, and diverse search toolset for prior-art search, reasoning, and OA generation. We propose PASS, i.e., Prior-Art Agentic Search Trajectory Synthesis, annotation-free framework that synthesizes high-quality prior-art search trajectories. By treating document visits as implicit relevance signals and evidence-acquisition anchors, PASS models intraand inter-turn search 2 Novel or Not? PatEx-Gym: Agentic Prior-Art Search for Novelty Assessment in Patent Examination behavior and progression, together with rollout-level evidence and outcome quality, yielding PatEx-SynData, which contains 3K filtered trajectories for agent training. Building on PatEx-SynData, we develop PatEx-Agent at 4B scale via SFT for prior-art search and novelty assessment in patent examination. Despite its compact scale, our PatEx-Agent exhibits strong performance and establishes lightweight baseline: the 4B variant performs comparably to models with 30B parameters and achieves Searched Recall (Search-R) on par with Qwen3.7Max. This also demonstrates the potential of lightweight agents for efficient local deployment in practical patent examination settings. 2. Related Work 2.1. Agentic Search and Deep Research Conventional information retrieval methods estimate the relevance between user query and documents in corpus, returning ranked list through lexical or learned matching functions [Burges et al., 2005, Robertson et al., 1994]. With the emergence of LLMs, search systems increasingly move beyond scoring for fixed query toward actively planning and adapting the search process [Li et al., 2025]. ReAct [Yao et al., 2023] and IRCoT [Trivedi et al., 2023] provide foundations for interleaving reasoning with environment actions or retrieval. Recent work further focuses on training search agents. Search-R1 [Jin et al., 2025] learns multi-turn reasoning and search through reinforcement learning and TIPS [Xie et al., 2026] leverage turn-level reward to optimize search-augmented LLMs. FORT-Searcher [Deng et al., 2026] constructs shortcut-resistant search tasks and trajectories. And SearchArt [Mei et al., 2026] combines verified task synthesis with multi-stage post-training. These methods formulate search as sequential decision process in which retrieved evidence informs subsequent queries and reasoning. Table 1 Comparison of patent examination benchmarks. Evidence Pool denotes the searchable candidates. Where PatEx-Bench comprises 1M patents and 52K papers. Reason denotes LLMs reasoning beyond retrieval alone; OA denotes Office Action generation; Agentic indicates whether provides harness for iterative tool use and multi-step task execution, and NPL denotes support for non-patent literature. Agentic search has further expanded to long-horizon Web research [Wei et al., 2025] and specialized document retrieval. Deep Research (DR) [Shi et al., 2025] represents prominent form of agentic search, in which agents conduct multi-step retrieval, synthesize evidence across sources, and produce citation-grounded answers or reports. Recent DR benchmarks and methods evaluate and train agents in terms of answer quality, citation correctness, and search behavior [Du et al., 2026a, Gou et al., 2026, Li et al., 2026, Team et al., 2025]. In specialized settings, PaperScout [Pan et al., 2026] dynamically combines direct search with citation expansion for academic literature retrieval. Patent examination requires search to support formal, claim-level decision under strict evidentiary and legal constraints. Our PatEx-Gym adapts the agentic search paradigm to patent examination, where agents search large-scale prior-art corpus and connect iterative evidence discovery with claim-level reasoning to produce traceable examination. 2,896 8 candidates no prior art 314 1,844 1 given document 480 PAR4PC IPBench Task 35 FiNE-Patents PatRe PatEx-Bench (Ours) 1,000 1M + 52K Reason OA Agentic NPL Test # Evidence Pool 10 references Benchmark 2.2. Patent Retrieval and Examination Prior-art retrieval is fundamental to patent examination, as reliable novelty assessments depend on identifying relevant earlier disclosures from massive patent collections. NTCIR Patent Retrieval [Fujii 3 Novel or Not? PatEx-Gym: Agentic Prior-Art Search for Novelty Assessment in Patent Examination et al., 2004] and CLEF-IP [Piroi et al., 2011] establish benchmarks for prior-art search, catalyzing advances in lexical retrieval, query expansion, cross-lingual matching, and patent-specific ranking. Within the broader examination process, retrieval is interleaved with query refinement, inspection of full disclosures, and reasoning that connects prior-art evidence to legally grounded decisions. Beyond ranking-based evaluation of prior-art retrievers [Fujii et al., 2004, Suzgun et al., 2023], recent benchmarks incorporate finer-grained evidence and reasoning into patent examination using LLMs [Wang et al., 2026a]. PANORAMA [Lim et al., 2025] decomposes claim-level examination into prior-art retrieval, paragraph identification, and novelty classification. However, these stages are evaluated separately and retrieval is restricted to small and fixed candidate pool. FiNE-Patents [Knappich et al., 2026] provides feature-level annotations for passage retrieval and novelty reasoning, but limited in given prior-art document. PatRe [Wang et al., 2026b] models OA generation and applicant rebuttal under various reference settings. As summarized in Table 1, PatEx-Bench advances toward an agentic paradigm by evaluating the complete searchreasoningassessment trajectory, where agents autonomously search across large-scale prior-art corpora. 3. PatEx-Bench In this section, we introduce PatEx-Bench, the first benchmark for evaluating agentic prior-art search and novelty assessment in patent examination scenario. Unlike settings in fixed candidate documents, PatEx-Bench requires an agent to autonomously discover temporally eligible patents and non-patent literature (NPL) and inspect their underlying disclosures. The agent must then reason over claims and produce an evidence-grounded novelty assessment in the form of traceable Office Action (OA). Each task runs in an isolated Codex harness that provides the workspace and toolsets over our large-scale Patent-1M and Paper-52K corpora. This design makes it possible to evaluate not only the final OA, but also the complete searchreasoningassessment trajectory. 3.1. Problem Definition Let = {𝑞𝑖}𝑁 𝑖=1 denote set of patent applications, and let = denote large-scale prior-art corpus consisting of patent documents and NPL (scientific papers). Each 𝑞𝑖 represents patent application and includes its bibliographic metadata, title, abstract, specification, claims, and filing date 𝑑𝑖. The agent decides whether to continue invoking tools or terminate the trajectory by submitting an OA 𝑜𝑖 and its reference set 𝑅𝑖 C𝑖. 3.2. Auditable Execution Harness Runtime As shown in Figure 1, we construct sandbox-based execution environment using harbor [Harbor Team, 2026], equipping them with diverse prior-art search toolset, including Boolean keyword 4 Novel or Not? PatEx-Gym: Agentic Prior-Art Search for Novelty Assessment in Patent Examination search, sparse retrieval (BM25 [Robertson et al., 1994]), and dense retrieval (BGE-M3 [Chen et al., 2024]), together with basic workspace tools, e.g., Read and Write. Notably, the search tools return only the bibliographic metadata, titles, and abstracts of documents. We further provide visit tools to support progressive disclosure of prior-art information, allowing agents to dynamically inspect documents they deem more relevant or potentially novelty-defeating and access richer content such as claims. Therefore, the agent primarily operates through 3 action types, Reasoning, Search, and Visit. Based on these tool designs, we integrate the search capabilities with the Codex [Chen, 2026] harness, enabling PatEx-Gym to support robust agentic runtimes. To ensure fair and reliable evaluation, we divide each agentic runtime into three strictly separated stages: Preparation, Execution, and Evaluation. During task execution, the agent has no access to the evaluation rubrics. Finally, the harness records the complete and auditable agent trajectory, search-tool execution logs, final environment state, and the requested artifacts. 3.3. Data Collection, Processing and Statistics Data Collection and Processing. PatEx-Bench is grounded in verifiable patent prosecution records sourced from publicly available USPTO research datasets , which contains examiner-authored OAs. As official examination decisions issued by qualified USPTO examiners, these OAs carry procedural legal effect and provide authoritative, professionally validated golden labels rather than synthetic annotations. For each 𝑞𝑖, we retain the first OA and the application in its originally filed version, including its bibliographic metadata, abstract, specification, and claims, ultimately yielding 1K tasks. This preserves the initial claims available to the agent instead of the final granted document. To support prior-art search, we further construct Patent-1M and Paper-52K from publicly accessible Google Patent and Scholar, respectively. We standardize heterogeneous identifiers and fields into unified schema and remove duplicate records. Notably, we verify that every examiner-cited oracle reference for each OA is retrievable from these two corpora. Data Statistics. Our PatEx-Bench comprises 1,000 patent examination tasks spanning all eight IPC sections, with 2,946 examiner-cited patents and 178 examiner-cited papers serving as groundtruth prior-art references. The Patent-1M and Paper-52K corpora contain 1,011,901 unique patent documents and 52,105 scientific papers, respectively. This poses substantial challenge for agents to efficiently discover and verify relevant prior art. As shown in Figure 2, we present the distributions of (a) IPC classifications, (b) temporal coverage, (c) decisions and statutory grounds, and (d) examinercited patent references for PatEx-Bench. 4. PatEx-SynData and PatEx-Agent Building upon the workspace environment of PatEx-Gym, we further investigate whether strong prior-art search capabilities can be acquired through agentic training. We propose PASS, scalable trajectory synthesis framework that generates prior-art search trajectories with teacher model and leverages document visits as implicit relevance signals to segment trajectories, model fine-grained 6 Novel or Not? We further use PASS to construct PatExSynData, curated training set of approximately 3K high-quality prior-art search trajectories selected from 10K teacher-generated rollouts. Based on PatEx-SynData, we train PatEx-Agent to acquire effective agentic search behaviors for prior-art discovery in realistic patent examination scenario. 4.1. Prior-Art Search Trajectory Synthesis In this section, we introduce PASS, i.e., Prior-Art Agentic Search Trajectory Synthesis, scalable, annotation-free framework that synthesizes prior-art search trajectories with teacher model using only structured patent documents as inputs, and curates them based on fine-grained quality at both the turn and trajectory levels. Specifically, as shown in Figure 3, PASS leverages the progressive disclosure of patent information through visit tools to enable visit-aware, turn-level trajectory quality ranking. It treats document visits as implicit relevance signals and evidence-acquisition anchors to capture both retrieval-to-inspection efficiency and evidence-driven search progression for novelty assessment in patent examination. 4.1.1. Visit-Guided Relevance-Aware Rollout Segmentation Given an application 𝑞𝑖, we employ teacher model to interact with the harness and generate complete prior-art search and OA generation trajectory 𝜏𝑖. This synthesis process is annotation-free and requires no examiner-cited references, enabling scalable trajectory generation directly from large-scale structured patent collections. In the progressive search-then-visit paradigm of PatEx-Gym, each visit not only reflects an implicit relevance judgment over the retrieved candidates [Zhou et al., 2026], analogous to clickthrough-based implicit feedback in Web search [Joachims et al., 2005], but also marks the acquisition of richer document-level evidence. Based on this observation, PASS views visit actions as natural anchors and performs visit-guided relevance-aware segmentation to decompose each raw trajectory 𝜏𝑖 into semantically coherent search turns, i.e., 𝜏𝑖 = {𝑇1, 𝑇2, . . . , 𝑇𝐾 }, 𝑇𝑘 = (cid:0)S𝑘, V𝑘(cid:1) . Agent Training 4.2.1. Data Recipes Given the annotation-free nature of PASS, we crawl 10K seed patents from the USPTO, balanced across all IPC sections and strictly disjoint from PatEx-Bench. Using the Codex harness of PatEx-Gym with the predefined search and visit tools, we synthesize trajectories by allowing the invoke tools, teacher model to reason, and generate outputs within the harness workspace, resulting in 10K training trajectories. Crucially, the teacher model has no access to the trajectory-quality evaluation criteria during generation. Then, we apply PASS to segment the rollouts and compute their turnand trajectory-level quality scores after filtering out invalid trajectories using Criterion 1. After filtering, we retain 6,321 trajectories within the admissible budget and rank them using the tournament-based procedure described in Section 4.1.3. Finally, we select the top 3K high-quality trajectories according to their tournament scores as the training data, termed PatEx-SynData. As shown in Fig. 4, we provide an overview of the PASS data curation process: (a) illustrates the progressive filtering of teachergenerated trajectories from the initial 10K seeds through the two selection criteria, while (b) presents the token-length and tool-call distributions of the resulting trajectories. Experiment 5.1. Experimental Setup Baselines. We evaluate 13 models spanning different families and parameter sizes, including (1) Frontier models: Claude-Opus-5, Claude-Opus-4.7, GLM-5.3, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 [Xu et al., 2026], Qwen3.7-Max, Qwen3.8-Max-0813 [Qwen Team, 2026a,b] and Kimi-K2.6; (2) Open-source models spanning both dense and MoE architectures across various parameter scales, including Qwen3.5-4/9/397A17B and Qwen3.6-27/35A3B. We also evaluate the retrieval performance of 12 retrievers and the agents on the patent corpus of our PatEx-Bench, including (1) Sparse Retriever: BM25 [Robertson et al., 1994], TF-IDF [Salton and Buckley, 1988], uniCOIL [Lin and Ma, 2021] and SPLADE-v3 [Lassance et al., 2024]; (2) Dense Retriever: BGE-M3 [Chen et al., 2024], jina-embeddingv5-text-nano/small [Akram et al., 2026], Qwen3-Embedding-0.6/4/8B [Zhang et al., 2025] and domain-specific models including PaECTER [Ghosh et al., 2024] and PatEmbed-Large [Ayaou and Cavallucci, 2025]. Implementations. For agent training, we optimize the SFT objective in Equation 9 using Qwen3.5-4B as the backbone and the PatEx-SynData synthesized by PASS with GLM-5.3 as the teacher model. We use the slime [Zhu et al., 2025] framework with reproducible configuration and train the model for 3 epochs on 8 NVIDIA H20 GPUs with learning rate of 1 105. For fair evaluation on PatEx-Bench, we use official APIs for closed-source models and larger open-source models, while deploying smaller models, such as Qwen3.5-9B, locally with the vLLM [Kwon et al., 2023]. All models are evaluated under the Codex (v0.151.0) with temperature of 1.0, maximum output length of 32,768 tokens, and maximum of 50 steps. The harness retains its native context-compaction mechanism. For models that support configurable reasoning effort, we use the highest available setting (e.g., xhigh or max), indicated by the corresponding postfix. We use the evaluation criteria defined in Section 3.3 to provide multi-dimensional assessment of prior-art search performance, averaging scores from 3 LLM judges, i.e., Claude-Opus-4.7, Gemini-3.5-Flash, and GPT-5.5. All judges use temperature of 0 and maximum output length of 8,192 tokens. 5.2. Main Results on PatEx-Bench As shown in Table 2, we report the performance of evaluated models on PatEx-Bench under the Codex harness. Overall, the agents exhibit substantial performance variation, with Scores ranging from 3.79 to 7.34. Claude-Opus-5-max achieves the best results in Score, Statute F1, and all three referencerecall metrics. The Select-R peaks at only 32.4, highlighting substantial room for improvement in statutory reasoning and prior-art search. Notably, despite its compact 4B scale, PatEx-Agent achieves Search-R of 38.7, surpassing larger models such as Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, while remaining competitive in OA quality. We further analyze the differences in terms of prior-art discovery and examination quality as follows. Strong models still face substantial prior-art discovery challenges. Claude-Opus-5-max achieves the highest OA quality Score at 7.34, together with the strongest statute identification and reference recall across all three retrieval stages. Nevertheless, even the strongest Search-R remains below 50% and Select-R below 33%, highlight the difficulty of discovering and retaining examiner-cited references through progressive search process. Notably, our PatEx-Agent substantially improves over its Qwen3.5-4B backbone, increasing the OA quality Score from 3.79 to 5.41 (+42.7%) and 10 Novel or Not? Qwen3.6-27B achieves the highest Decision Accuracy of 87.6%, yet its Score and Select-R remain substantially below those of ClaudeOpus-5-max, at 5.96 vs. 7.34 and 19.5 vs. 32.4, respectively. These results indicate that correct final decisions do not necessarily imply equally strong prior-art discovery or overall OA quality. Additionally, we compute the agreement among the three LLM judges, obtaining Kendalls 𝑊 = 0.849, which demonstrates strong consistency in their quality rankings and supports the reliability of our LLM-based evaluation. This discrepancy suggests that retrieving relevant references is only part of the challenge: agents must also identify useful documents among search results and incorporate them into the final examination. In contrast, our PatEx-Agent improves Search-R from 23.2 to 38.7 (+66.8%) while Select-R from 12.0 to 18.2 (+51.7%) over its backbone. The disproportionate gain in Select-R suggests that PatEx-Agent improves not only search coverage, but also the ability to convert retrieved evidence into selected references used in the examination. 5.3. Its performance remains highly competitive at later stages, reaching 37.6 Visit-R and 27.7 Select-R and outperforming many substantially larger models. This suggests that the learned search behavior generalizes beyond patent retrieval to NPL. 5.4. Ablation Study 5.4.1. Ablation on Trajectory Sampling Strategy To isolate the effect of trajectory selection, we randomly sample 3K trajectories from the same generated pool, matching the size of PatEx-SynData, and train the same backbone with identical settings. Random sampling provides only limited and inconsistent gains over the Qwen3.54B base model. In particular, random sampling reduces R@10 from 14.9 to 11.6 (-22.1%) and R@20 from 19.2 to 17.1 (-10.9%), while Select-R also drops slightly from 12.03 to 11.96 (-0.6%). In contrast, training on PASS-filtered trajectories raises Select-R to 18.24 (+51.6%). Under the same data budget and training procedure, this gap highlights the importance of PASSs multidimensional quality assessment helps select trajectories that teach the agent to turn retrieved candidates into useful final evidence, rather than relying on fine-tuning alone. Figure 6 Ablation of sampling strategies for prior-art search. 5.4.2. Ablation on Search Toolset We conduct search-tool ablation study by isolating the Boolean, BM25, and BGE-M3 retriever, with only one enabled. As shown in Fig. 7 (left), the full toolset provides the strongest retrieval performance, while Boolean-only search causes the More largest degradation. importantly, under the same Boolean-only constraint, our PatEx-Agent improves Search-R from 10.08 to 25.12 (+149.2%) and Visit-R from 6.35 to 16.14 (+154.2%) over the backbone. This indicates that PatEx-Agent learns more effective query construction and search behavior from the PatEx-SynData rather than merely relying on strong tool. Among the isolated tools, BGE-M3 performs best and allows PatEx-Agent to nearly recover its full-tool performance in Search-R (37.24 vs. 38.70) and 𝑅@100 (35.82 vs. 36.36). Nevertheless, the full toolset remains stronger in Search-R and Select-R, suggesting that Boolean, lexical, and dense retrieval provide complementary coverage. The left example retains relevant prior art through search, inspection, and selection, while the right example retrieves the relevant reference but fails to use it in the final evidence set. 5.4.3. Ablation on Semantic Search Tool We replace the dense retriever while remains the other tools, comparing BGE-M3 with Qwen3Embedding-0.6B and PatEmbed-Large. As shown in Figure 7 (right), stronger retrievers generally improve recalls, but these gains do not always translate into better Select-R. For Qwen3.5-4B, PatEmbed-Large increases Search-R from 23.20 to 24.60 and R@100 from 24.06 to 24.78, while Select-R slightly decreases from 12.00 to 11.60. This may indicate that stronger retriever introduces more similar candidates, making evidence selection more difficult. 5.5. Case Study We provide detailed case study with two contrasting examples in Figure 8, covering successful prior-art retention and failure to use retrieved evidence in the final decision. (I) In the left example, we observe successful pipeline: the agent decomposes the claim into complementary concepts, reformulates its query across retrieval tools, verifies candidate prior-art, and assigns distinct evidentiary roles before generating the OA. It preserves the oracle reference throughout the SearchVisitSelect funnel and yields the correct decision and statutory ground. (II) In the right example, we observe different pattern in which the agent retrieves the oracle reference but does not promote it to document inspection or final selection. Its statutory prediction is incomplete but does not introduce incorrect grounds. Together, these examples show that effective agentic examination requires both iterative search and disciplined evidence selection: broad retrieval can expose the necessary prior art, but only verified and correctly selected novelty-aware evidence can support complete legal conclusion. 6. Conclusion In this work, we introduced PatEx-Gym, unified framework for developing and evaluating agentic patent examination models, including PatEx-Bench, PASS for synthesizing PatEx-SynData, and the Novel or Not? PatEx-Gym: Agentic Prior-Art Search for Novelty Assessment in Patent Examination lightweight baseline PatEx-Agent. Our extensive experiments show that final decision accuracy alone cannot fully capture examination quality, and that prior-art discovery, evidence inspection, and final selection remain challenging even for strong frontier models. Despite its 4B scale, our PatEx-Agent substantially improves over its base model and achieves prior-art discovery performance comparable to agents with 30B size. These findings identify evidence inspection and selection as central challenges for agentic search and deep research. Moreover, we believe that effective agents must go beyond document search to coordinate adaptive querying, tool-use, evidence integration, and reasoning throughout the search process. We hope our PatEx-Gym provides realistic testbed for advancing evidence-grounded agentic search and deep research.
